conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. I spend my days talking with new mothers about the emotional ups-and-downs that can arrive alongside a brand-new baby.

Today I’d like to do a quick screening tool called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within your medical record. Our goal is to make sure you feel heard, supported, and—if necessary—connected to the right resources so you can enjoy these early weeks with your baby.

We’ll go through the questions one by one. Most moms finish in just a few minutes, and you can take your time on each item. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Let’s start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… I still laugh sometimes, but it feels like I have to work harder to find that funny side. Even when my husband jokes around, it doesn’t come as naturally as it used to. I’d say I’ve been laughing, just not with the same ease.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh… but it’s not the same easy, automatic thing it was before the baby. It feels like I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even then the laughter fades pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to help or when we get to take the baby for a short walk—but the excitement feels kind of dulled. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than the bubbly, can’t-wait feeling I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like when she wouldn’t settle after her 2 a.m. feeding and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not burping her right or I ate something that’s bothering her. My head tells me babies just cry, but I still catch myself thinking it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A couple of nights I’ve lain in bed with my heart racing, running through all the “what-ifs” about her breathing or whether she’s gaining enough weight. Nothing specific happened to trigger it—she was sleeping fine—so I guess that counts as “no good reason.” It isn’t constant, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but I do get these sudden waves of “what if something’s wrong and I don’t notice?”—like a little jolt of fear that makes my chest tight. It’s quick, maybe a minute or two, and then it fades. It’s happened maybe twice in the past week, always when the baby’s asleep and the house is too quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… some days it feels like the second I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, laundry—there’s already another pile waiting. I’m not falling apart, but I do get that “how am I going to keep up?” feeling, especially in the evenings when I’m running on a few broken hours of sleep.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” but I do feel keyed-up and kind of heavy at the same time once the lights go out. That’s when my mind starts replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying I missed something, and then I’m staring at the ceiling for an hour or more. It’s happened three or four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get waves of sadness—usually when I’m alone with her in the late afternoon and the house feels quiet and gray. It’s not all day, and I still have okay moments, but yeah, I’ve caught myself tearing up and just feeling kind of empty a few times in the past week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t had those big, can’t-stop tears—just a couple of times my eyes welled up and one quick cry in the shower on Thursday. It passed pretty fast. So I’ve felt weepy, but not completely overwhelmed by it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and low, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that since your baby arrived you still manage to laugh and look forward to small moments, yet the joy feels dulled and fleeting. You described waves of sadness that roll in during quiet afternoons, worries about your daughter's wellbeing that make your heart race at night, and a sense that the everyday tasks are piling up faster than you can manage. These feelings are understandably upsetting, and many new mothers experience similar struggles as hormones, sleep loss, and the huge life change of parenting blend together.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh, needing to consciously remind herself and finding the feeling fleeting, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enthusiasm ("dulled," "that'll be nice" vs. past "bubbly, can't-wait"), clearly matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>She endorses self-blame "a few times this week" and gives a clear example, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring nighttime anxiety episodes without triggers, happening "a few times a week," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports discrete waves of fear/tight chest without trigger, occurring twice in the week — fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most days') and difficulty keeping up, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient denies extreme unhappiness but describes nightly anxiety-driven insomnia most of the week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent waves of sadness, tearfulness, and emptiness several times in the past week, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 17 (≥14 indicates probable major depression). Key symptoms align with DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym> and guilt, <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym> (racing heart), <sym>fatigue</sym>/<sym>loss of energy</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> despite infant sleeping, and <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym>. <quote>I do get waves of sadness-usually when I'm alone with her in the late afternoon</quote>. Patient denies suicidal ideation (Q10 score 0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric or primary care provider</med> within one week for full evaluation and possible medication or therapy referral
2. Schedule EPDS re-screen or phone check-in within 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
3. Encourage immediate <med>CBT-based</med> or interpersonal postpartum support group; provide local/telehealth options
4. Offer practical help plan: enlist family/friends for night shifts, meal trains, or household chores to increase sleep blocks
5. Teach 5-minute breathing or grounding exercise for racing-heart episodes; demonstrate now if time allows
6. Provide 24-h crisis hotline numbers and instruct to call if mood worsens or any thought of self-harm emerges
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style questionnaire, 10 self-report items (2–3 weeks postpartum).

Areas endorsed above threshold / clinical concern  
- Persistent low mood and anhedonia (items 1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (item 3)  
- Generalized anxiety and nocturnal panic symptoms (items 4, 5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and coping difficulty (item 6)  
- Sleep-onset disturbance linked to rumination (item 7)  
- Absence of suicidal or self-harm ideation (item 10)

Pattern summary  
Patient describes diminution of pleasure in previously enjoyable activities, intermittent tearfulness, late-afternoon “empty” spells, and recurrent intrusive worries about infant well-being. Episodes of autonomic arousal (racing heart, chest tightness) occur 2–3×/week at rest. Sleep is fragmented by psychogenic insomnia rather than infant demands. Functioning is maintained, but she reports feeling “keyed-up and heavy” and questions her capacity to “keep up.”

Screening significance  
Findings are consistent with mild-moderate postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features. No safety concerns identified at present.

Next steps discussed  
Recommended follow-up screening in 1–2 weeks and psychoeducation on postpartum mood/anxiety disorders; voluntary referral to obstetric/postpartum behavioral health for further evaluation.
